newsitem.title: USA: White House urges restraint after IRA bomb attack.
newsitem.headline: White House urges restraint after IRA bomb attack.

text.p: The White House urged British loyalists in Northern Ireland on Tuesday not to be provoked to bloodshed by an IRA bomb attack on British Army headquarters there.

"The United States condemns in the strongest terms yesterday's barbaric attack on the military base at Lisburn in Northern Ireland, which injured over 30 people," White House press secretary Mike McCurry said in a statement.

"These acts of terrorism must not be allowed to derail the important work of peace occurring in Belfast under the chairmanship of (former U.S.) Senator (George) Mitchell and his two colleagues," he said.

President Bill Clinton's national security adviser Anthony Lake said he feared a return to full-scale violence in the streets of Northern Ireland would destroy the future of the province and the peace process, for which many including the Clinton administration have worked.

Lake said the bombers may have intended "to wave a red flag and try ... to get the loyalist bull to run through the cape and start again the troubles," Lake said of the dual car bombs at British barracks that injured 31 people on Monday.
"That would be a tragic, tragic decision," Lake said.
He said he had "deep and sincere admiration" for the loyalists who have held to a ceasefire in the face of renewed violence by the Irish Republican Army since last February.
Lake added that if the loyalists, who favour continued British rule of the province while the IRA is fighting to end it, rejoined the conflict, "it could destroy the future of Northern Ireland."
McCurry also praised the "courage and determination the loyalists have shown in resisting provocation and refusing to be drawn into the spiral of violence."
Lake, a central figure in the Clinton administration's Northern Ireland policy, made his comments in a speech at Georgetown University and in remarks to reporters later.

The IRA on Tuesday claimed responsibility for the blasts at Lisburn near Belfast. It was the first time the IRA had struck at a security target in Northern Ireland since ending a 17-month ceasefire in February.

In his remarks to students, Lake said the attack was "despicable" and "an outrageous act of terrorism." He said it "deserves the strongest possible condemnation by civilised men and women everywhere."
"Those responsible must be brought to justice and as soon as possible," he said.
He urged all sides to press ahead with peace talks, which began in June and are mediated by Mitchell.

He said the Clinton administration, which has made settling the Northern Ireland conflict a top priority, would do all it could to keep the peace process on track. And he repeated earlier U.S. condemnations of IRA violence.

"The president and the American people remain deeply outraged by the IRA's breach of the ceasefire, its vicious bomb attacks in London and Manchester, and its continuing attempts to maim and kill innocent civilians," he said.

Lake said he had not been in touch with Gerry Adams, the leader of Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing, since the Monday bombing. Clinton's decision to issue Adams a U.S. visa early in 1994 helped lead to the IRA's declaration of a ceasefire later that year.

Lake said the United States would like to see Sinn Fein at the peace talks but only once it had restored the ceasefire. Britain and Ireland have insisted on an end to IRA violence as a condition of Sinn Fein's entry into the talks.

Lake repeated the White House's insistence that it does not seek to impose its own solution in Northern Ireland but just to facilitate a settlement. "We are neither in favour of a united Ireland nor opposed to the idea."
Clinton visited Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland last November and was greeted by cheering crowds. He is reported to be considering another visit to the region late this year.
